title: Ang 966–968: Satta and Balvand
hook: the minstrels' ballad of the Gurus' light
tomorrow: how does a boy fly a kite and still keep God in mind?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ang 957: the fifth Guru's ballad, and two people at a wedding holding the hem of the One. Today, a ballad sung by two musicians.
screen: `HOLDING THE HEM.` → `A BALLAD BY TWO MUSICIANS.`

segments.voice: Band breakups make the best documentaries: two musicians, a lot of talent, and one fight nobody tells the same way. Ang 966 holds a ballad by two musicians, Satta and Balvand, minstrels who played for the Gurus. Their var praises the Gurus' light. And around it, tradition tells the story of a falling-out. So today's question isn't who was right in the fight. It's how to read the song.
screen: `A BAND BREAKS UP.` → `SATTA AND BALVAND.` → `A BALLAD, AND A FALLING-OUT.`

segments.voice: First, the text. On ang 966, in paraphrase: the light is the same, the way is the same; the Master has only changed the body. That's how Satta and Balvand sing the guruship passing from Guru Nanak to Guru Angad and on: one light, new bodies. Now the story. Tradition says the two minstrels, proud of their art, quarreled with Guru Arjan and walked away; that they suffered for it, came back humbled through a devoted Sikh's pleading, and were forgiven. Here's where readers part ways. The first voice says: the story is the key. Hear the var through it, and it's a song of pride and mercy, two men who walked out and came back to sing the Gurus' light. Its best case: the Granth kept the song of people who failed, which says a great deal about forgiveness. The second voice says: the var itself tells none of that. No quarrel, no curse, no return. Its best case: read what's on the page. The ballad is praise, steady and bright, and a later story shouldn't color the hymn. Both voices are honest about something. And both stand on the same line at the center: bodies change; the light doesn't. There's something fitting in who sings it, too. Not a Guru, but two musicians, giving the Granth one of its clearest pictures of the guruship. The light passes.
screen: `ON THE PAGE: THE SAME LIGHT.` · `THE STORY: A QUARREL, FORGIVEN.` · `READ IT WITH THE STORY.` · `READ ONLY THE PAGE.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT PASSES.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers the people who passed something on to you: a recipe, a skill, a way of laughing, a line of prayer. One finger for each, with a slow breath for each name. When your fingers run out, rest your hands and stay with whatever light came through them.
Ang 966. Where Satta and Balvand's ballad stands: two minstrels singing one light passed from Guru to Guru.
The light passes: the same light, the same way, only a new body carrying it. Ballad sung.

howItsDone: Ragis sing the var of Satta and Balvand in Ramkali; it is often quoted for its line that the light and the way are the same, with only the body changed, from Guru to Guru.
